title: The tailor's accounting
hook: a tailor tells God: I sinned a little, You let children suffer; let us forgive each other

segments.voice: Yesterday, Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev stood before God as his people's defense attorney. Your line was always the defense. Did you speak up for someone? Today, the same rebbe overhears a tailor who argues even harder. Day three hundred one.

Picture the synagogue in Berditchev on Yom Kippur. Hours into the fast. Hundreds of people tapping their chests, reading the long lists of sins from the prayer book. The rebbe, Levi Yitzchak, is watching the room. And one man in the back, a tailor, isn't reading at all. He's talking to God, quietly, the way you'd talk to a business partner across a kitchen table. The rebbe walks over to listen. What he hears is one of the boldest prayers in all the Hasidic tales. And the rebbe's reaction is even more surprising.
screen: `YOM KIPPUR IN BERDITCHEV.` → `A TAILOR, NOT READING.` → `TALKING TO GOD LIKE A PARTNER.`

segments.voice: Here's what the tailor says, as the story is told. Master of the world, I've done wrong. Sometimes I kept the leftover scraps of cloth. Once or twice I ate without washing my hands. Small things. But You. You have taken babies from their mothers, and mothers from their babies. So let's make an accounting. You forgive me, and I'll forgive You. Let's call it even. People hearing this for the first time tend to gasp. Can anyone talk to God like that? Levi Yitzchak doesn't scold him. In the telling, the rebbe's only complaint is that the tailor settled too cheaply. With an argument like that, he says, you could have demanded that God redeem the whole Jewish people. Why isn't this blasphemy? Because it stands in a very old line. Abraham argued with God over Sodom: "shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" Moses argued. Job argued for chapters. The Hebrew word for an accounting is cheshbon, and before Yom Kippur Jews make a cheshbon ha-nefesh, an accounting of the soul. The tailor simply turned the ledger both ways. The story doesn't explain why children suffer. Jewish tradition has wrestled with that question for thousands of years, and many of its voices admit there's no easy answer. This story doesn't pretend to have one. What it does is refuse to fake it. You only argue with someone you believe is listening. And it closes a week of Hasidic tales: the shepherd boy's whistle, the alphabet prayer, the fire and the place, Zusya, two pockets, the defense attorney, and today, the tailor's accounting.
screen: `I KEPT THE SCRAPS.` · `YOU FORGIVE ME, I FORGIVE YOU.` · `ABRAHAM ARGUED TOO.` · `CHESHBON: AN HONEST ACCOUNTING.` · then, large: `LET'S CALL IT EVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be honest with God, or with yourself, if that's the word that fits you. Settle, and breathe. Let one thing come up that you've been too polite to say. A loss that made no sense. A hope that went unanswered. A hurt you keep covering with good manners. You don't have to fix it or explain it. Just say it plainly, inside, the way the tailor did. If you pray, you can say it to God. Then breathe, and let it sit there, said. The bell holds the time.
The tailor's accounting. A Yom Kippur bargain from Berditchev: You forgive me, I forgive You. Honesty, in the one place people expect only apology.
Your line: let's call it even. Today, when you're tempted to smooth something over with a polite answer, tell the truth instead, and tell it kindly. Day three hundred one.

howItsDone: Hasidic communities retell stories like the tailor's around Yom Kippur, and many Jews make a cheshbon ha-nefesh, an honest accounting of the soul, in the weeks before the day.

fork.setup: you're the rebbe. on Yom Kippur you overhear a tailor offering God a deal: I'll forgive You if You forgive me. what do you say?
fork.reveal: in the story, Levi Yitzchak says the tailor could have demanded the redemption of the whole people. he pushes the argument further, not back.

original.note: Hebrew: an accounting of the soul, the stock-taking many Jews do before Yom Kippur.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheeky joke about a tailor.
what it means: an honest prayer that says the hard thing out loud, and a rebbe who takes it seriously.
what a scholar hears: the tailor's cheshbon runs in a line back to Abraham at Sodom, and the tale exists in several versions with different rebbes and details.

notes: The tale is told in several versions (some attach it to other rebbes; details of the tailor's small sins vary). Confirm the attribution to Levi Yitzchak and the rebbe's reply ('you settled too cheaply; you could have demanded redemption').
The line 'You have taken babies from their mothers' is the common form of the tailor's complaint; a Keeper may prefer a gentler rendering for younger listeners.
Genesis 18:25 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm exact wording and capitalization.
